definition: The geometry that limits where an analysis runs, such as Bhutan's national boundary or one Dzongkhag.
The area of each land use or land-use change (for example hectares of deforestation) in a period. In carbon reporting it is multiplied by emission factors to give emissions.
An Earth Engine stack of images (ee.ImageCollection), such as all Sentinel-2 scenes, that can be filtered by place, date and metadata.
One image built from many by taking a per-pixel statistic, such as the median, to remove clouds and noise.
An Earth Engine object (ee.Reducer) that summarises many values into one, across images, pixels in a region, or neighbourhoods.
Normalised Difference Vegetation Index, (NIR − Red) / (NIR + Red); higher values mean more green vegetation.
A mask that hides pixels flagged as cloud or cloud shadow so they do not affect composites or classifications.
An input band used by a classifier, such as a spectral band, an index, elevation or slope.
A machine-learning classifier that combines the votes of many decision trees, each trained on a random sample of the data and covariates.
In RLCMS, a probability layer (0–100) for one land-cover class, produced by a classifier and later combined into a map by assemblage rules.
Combining primitives into a single land-cover map with ordered decision-tree rules and thresholds.
Regional Land Cover Monitoring System: the SERVIR primitives-and-assemblage approach to consistent land-cover mapping.
A 64-dimensional vector per 10 m pixel and year (Google's Satellite Embedding dataset, from AlphaEarth Foundations) that summarises the pixel's multi-sensor time series.
A map class used to divide the area for sampling, such as stable forest, stable non-forest or deforestation.
A table that cross-tabulates map classes against reference classes at sample points; the basis of accuracy and area estimates.
The share of samples mapped as a class that really are that class (1 − commission error).
The share of samples that really are a class and were mapped as it (1 − omission error).
The area of a class estimated from the reference sample and the stratum weights (Olofsson et al. 2014), rather than by counting map pixels.
A range expected to contain the true value with a stated probability; this course reports areas with 90% confidence intervals.
A free web tool for interpreting sample plots on high-resolution imagery, used to label the reference sample.

Reducing Emissions from Deforestation and forest Degradation, plus conservation, sustainable management of forests and enhancement of forest carbon stocks: the UNFCCC framework for rewarding countries that keep forests standing.
Measurement, reporting and verification: measuring forest change and emissions, reporting them in a set format, and having an independent body check them.
The emissions (or removals) per hectare of a land-cover change, such as tonnes of CO₂ per hectare deforested. Multiplied by activity data, it gives total emissions.
An independent check, by an accredited body, that reported results follow the standard and are supported by evidence.
The conversion of forest land to another land use, such as cropland or settlement.
A loss of carbon stock or forest condition while the land stays forest, for example from selective logging or fire.
Land that was forest at both the start and the end of the period.
Google's cloud platform for analysing satellite imagery and geospatial data with JavaScript or Python, without downloading the data.
The browser-based Earth Engine programming environment at code.earthengine.google.com, with a script panel, map, Console, Inspector and Tasks tab.
A dataset stored in Earth Engine, such as an exported image or an uploaded shapefile, addressed by a path like projects/<your-project>/assets/…
The Google Cloud project that an Earth Engine account works under. It owns your assets and is named in ee.Initialize(project=…) in Python.
A raster in Earth Engine: one or more bands with the same footprint, plus properties.
One layer of an image, such as Sentinel-2's near-infrared band B8.
A geometry with properties, such as a sample point with its class label.
A set of features, such as the Dzongkhag boundaries or a table of training points.
A point, line or polygon in Earth Engine, with coordinates in longitude and latitude by default.
A rule that keeps only some elements of a collection, such as images from one date range or inside the area of interest.
Applying the same function to every element of a collection with .map(). The function must return an Earth Engine object.
Your browser or notebook (the client) builds instructions; Google's servers run them. Server objects such as ee.Number have no value in the browser until printed or exported.
A batch task that saves a result as an asset, a Drive file or a Cloud Storage file. It runs from the Tasks tab and has higher limits than interactive requests.
The pixel size, in metres, at which Earth Engine computes or exports a result.
The coordinate reference system of an image, such as EPSG:4326 (latitude/longitude) or EPSG:32645 (UTM zone 45N).
A per-pixel flag that hides pixels from display and analysis, such as cloud, shadow or non-forest pixels.
The share of incoming sunlight that a surface reflects in a given wavelength, from 0 to 1. Earth Engine often stores it scaled, for example multiplied by 10,000.
Reflectance corrected for the atmosphere, as if measured at the ground (Sentinel-2 Level-2A, Landsat Level-2).
How the reflectance of a surface changes across wavelengths. Vegetation reflects little red light and much near-infrared light.
A formula combining bands to highlight one property, such as NDVI for green vegetation or NDWI for water.
Light just beyond red (about 0.75–1.4 µm), strongly reflected by healthy leaves.
Light at about 1.4–3 µm, sensitive to water in leaves and soil and useful for separating burned, bare and built land.
The ground size of one pixel: 10 m for Sentinel-2's visible and NIR bands, 30 m for Landsat.
How often a satellite images the same place: about 5 days for the two Sentinel-2 satellites, 8 days for Landsat 8 and 9 together.
The European Space Agency's pair of multispectral satellites (2A, 2B and now 2C), imaging since 2015 at 10–60 m.
The NASA/USGS series of satellites, imaging the Earth since 1972. The course uses Landsat 8 and 9 at 30 m.
A Google dataset that scores every Sentinel-2 pixel for how clear it is, used to mask cloud and shadow.
Adjusting reflectance for slope and aspect so that sunlit and shaded hillsides of the same cover look alike; the course uses the SCS+C method.
Temporal Dark Outlier Mask: flags pixels much darker than usual in the NIR and SWIR bands, which are likely cloud shadow.
Correcting for how reflectance changes with the sun and view angles, so images taken at different angles match.
A composite that takes, for each pixel and band, the median of all clear observations, which removes most remaining cloud and shadow.
A raster of ground height, such as SRTM at 30 m, used for terrain correction and terrain covariates (elevation, slope, aspect).
Labelled points or polygons used to teach a classifier what each class looks like. They are not the same as the reference sample used for accuracy assessment.
An algorithm that learns from training data to assign a class or probability to every pixel, such as Random Forest.
A classifier output giving, for each pixel, the estimated probability (0–100) that it belongs to one class. RLCMS primitives are probability layers.
A set of yes/no rules applied in order. The RLCMS assemblage uses one to turn primitives into a single land-cover map.
When a model learns the noise in its training data and does well on it but poorly on new data.
A measure from −1 to 1 of how alike two vectors are. Satellite Embedding vectors have unit length, so it equals their dot product.
The six land-use categories of the IPCC guidelines: forest land, cropland, grassland, wetlands, settlements and other land. The course's classes follow them.
The best available labels for the sample, made by interpreting high-resolution imagery or by field visits, and treated as the truth when assessing accuracy.
A sample in which every unit has a known, non-zero chance of selection, which allows unbiased estimates.
Dividing the area into strata, often the map classes, and drawing a random sample in each.
How the total sample size is divided among strata: proportional to area, equal, or with a minimum per stratum.
The estimated standard deviation of an estimate across repeated samples: a measure of its precision.
Half the width of a confidence interval, such as ±2,459 ha for a 90% interval.
The estimated share of the map area that is correctly classified.
Area mapped as a class that is really something else; equal to 1 − user's accuracy.
Area of a class that the map missed; equal to 1 − producer's accuracy.
How far the true value may lie from the estimate, usually reported as a confidence interval or as its half-width relative to the estimate.
One of Bhutan's 20 districts; the first administrative level below the country.
Google's annual 64-band, 10 m embedding images made by the AlphaEarth Foundations model, available in Earth Engine from 2017.
